Sentinel at work

Sentinel is a system that watches trading in a simulated stock market and looks for traders who are trying to cheat. Below you can watch real replays from it, try to spot the cheating yourself, and then see what Sentinel decided and why.

1. A market is a queue of offers

Some people have offered to buy at a price (blue). Others have offered to sell (orange). A trade happens when a buy and a sell meet. Anyone can cancel an offer at any moment. The picture of all waiting offers is called the order book.

2. Some traders cheat

Because everyone reads the order book to judge demand, a cheat can fake it: a huge offer they never mean to fill (spoofing), a staircase of them (layering), or trading with themselves to fake activity (wash trading).

3. Sentinel watches for the pattern

Every 10 seconds, for every trader, it measures 22 behaviours (how big their orders are, how fast they cancel, who they trade with) and decides if the pattern looks like cheating, and it tells you why.

New to trading terms? Open the glossary
Order
An offer to buy or sell some number of shares at a price.
Bid / ask
A bid is an offer to buy. An ask is an offer to sell.
Tick
The smallest price step. Prices here are shown in ticks (like 9,978).
Spread
The gap between the best buy price and the best sell price.
Middle price
Halfway between the best buy and best sell price. When it moves, the market thinks the value changed.
Cancel
Withdrawing an offer before anyone has traded with it.
Market maker
A firm that always offers to both buy and sell, so others can trade. It cancels and re-posts constantly, which is normal.
Window
A 10-second slice of one trader's activity. Sentinel scores one window at a time.
Alert
Sentinel saying "this window looks like cheating", together with the reasons.
Simulated
Every trade here is from a computer-simulated market, so cheating cases can be planted and known for certain.

Pick a story

These replays come from a simulation the model never saw during training. The four caught cases were chosen as clear examples, and the fifth is a deliberate miss. Overall, on a separate untouched test simulation, Sentinel catches about 29% of manipulation windows while wrongly flagging about 0.4% of innocent ones, and on the hardest cases it catches only a few percent. The full numbers are in RESULTS.md.
